newsitem.title: USA: U.S. upbeat on N.Korea talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. upbeat on N.Korea talks.

text.p: Negotiators for the United States and both Koreas met on Wednesday to discuss a landmark peace talks proposal as U.S. officials voiced new optimism that Pyongyang was nearing agreement on negotiations.

U.S. officials told Reuters the three sides had been "fine tuning" an announcement that would commit North Korea to attending a senior-level meeting that would set an agenda and other details for the peace talks, proposed by Washington and Seoul more than one year ago.
A senior U.S. official said that during meetings in New York over the past month "we've chipped away bit by bit and narrowed these differences so now we are very close."
"Whether we will be able to close the remaining gap in one more session or two more sessions or 10 more sessions, I would tend to think one or two might do it," he added.

State Department spokesman John Dinger described Wednesday's meeting as "useful" and said "we expect to continue our discussions." He gave no details. "We believe the talks are headed in the right direction," he said.
The peace talks aim to close the books on the 1950-53 Korean War by replacing a fraying armistice with a permanent treaty between South Korea and the Stalinist North.
The senior official who was interveiwed on condition of anonymity said he expected, once a deal was clinched, the three sides would hold a senior-level meeting to confirm the accord.
The peace talks could begin in earnest by early August with a preparatory meeting in which negotiators decide the agenda and other details like venue and timing, he said.
That is the point at which China, North Korea's chief ally and the fourth party to the talks, would enter the process.
Although U.S. officials say progress has been made in getting North Korea to the table, they remain somewhat cautious because of previous experience with Pyongyang.

During a three-way senior-level meeting in New York last April, famine-threatened North Korea agreed in principle to join four-nation peace talks but queered a final deal by making its participation conditional on large-scale food aid and an easing of U.S. trade sanctions.
Washington and Seoul refused these conditions although both governments have donated most of the 1997 international food aid to North Korea totalling almost 500,000 tons.

The two allies distinguish between humanitarian aid -- which responds to World Food Programme (WFP) appeals and which Washington and Seoul are willing to provide now -- and other financial aid that will only flow after peace talks start.
Food remains Pyongyang's main preoccupation.
"What the North Koreans still want is as much of a commitment as they can get on whether or not we intend to use food as a weapon against them in these (peace) talks," a U.S. official said.

"We've been telling them over and over that isn't how we use food. We have stepped up to every food crisis around the world without exception" and will continue to respond to WFP humanitarian appeals for North Korea, he added.
The WFP is expected to make another appeal for North Korea, perhaps as early as this week, U.S. officials said.
As part of the deal now taking shape, South Korea has promised North Korea "substantial" new financial assistance once it enters peace talks, the senior U.S. official said.
The offer is a "little vague" but is would include more food aid, investment and other economic assistance, he said.

This assistance "is not going to come to North Korea just for coming (to peace talks) and then thumbing their nose and making a mockery of the process nor is it required that we get through the whole process and reach (final) agreement on a peace treaty" before assistance flows, the official said.

Rather, as the negotiations proceed and "the South Korean public becomes more comfortable with the notion that North Korea is engaged in an effort to create permanent peace, then the South Korean public will be more comfortable with the idea of helping North Korea in a fairly substantial way," he said.
